function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends an HTTP GET request to retrieve Device Connector Versions information from a specified URL. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The URL to which the GET request is sent. The URL points to a JSON file containing Device Connector Versions information.

params.description: Optional query parameters to include in the GET request as key-value pairs.

message.content:
Getting detailed information for a network interface depends on the platform you’re working with and the tools you have available. Below are some common ways to pull that data, along with example commands or API calls. If you let me know the exact device type (Cisco IOS/IOS‑XE, Juniper JUNOS, Arista EOS, Linux, Windows, etc.) I can tailor the instructions even more precisely. --- ## 1. **Command‑Line Interface (CLI)** | Platform | Typical command | Example output snippet | |----------|-----------------|------------------------| | **Cisco IOS / IOS‑XE** | `show interface `
or `show interface detail` | ``` is up, line protocol is up
Hardware is , address is (bia )
MTU 1500 bytes, BW 100000 Kbit/s, DLY 10 usec
Encapsulation ARPA, loopback not set``` | | **Juniper JUNOS** | `show interfaces terse`
or `show interfaces extensive` | ``` is up, line protocol is up
Physical interface: , MTU 1500, Speed 1G, Duplex full``` | | **Arista EOS** | `show interface status`
or `show interface counters` | ``` is up, line protocol is up
Link speed 1G, duplex full, MTU 1500``` | | **Linux** | `ip -d link show `
or `ifconfig ` | ```: mtu 1500 qdisc pfifo_fast state UP mode DEFAULT group default qlen 1000
link/ether brd ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff``` | | **Windows** | `Get-NetAdapter -Name ""` (PowerShell) | ```Name : Ethernet0
InterfaceDescription : Intel(R) Ethernet Connection
Status : Up
MacAddress : 00-1A-2B-3C-4D-5E``` | ### How to use: 1. **Open a terminal or console session** to the device (SSH, console cable, remote desktop, etc.). 2. **Enter the appropriate command** for your platform. 3. **Review the output** – it will include: * Operational status (up/down) * Physical attributes (speed, duplex, MTU) * MAC address * Counters (bytes, packets, errors) * Link-layer encapsulation * VLAN membership (if applicable) --- ## 2. **SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol)** If you prefer to script or integrate into monitoring software, SNMP can expose the same data via OIDs. | Data | Common OID | Notes | |------|------------|-------| | Interface description | `1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.2.` | `ifDescr` | | Status | `1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.8.` | `ifOperStatus` | | Speed | `1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.5.` | `ifSpeed` | | MTU | `1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.4.` | `ifMtu` | | MAC address | `1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.6.` | `ifPhysAddress` | | Counters | `1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.10.` (inOctets), `1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.16.` (outOctets) | | **Example SNMP walk (using `snmpwalk`):** ```bash snmpwalk -v2c -c public 192.168.1.1 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.2 ``` This will list all interface descriptions; you can then query specific indices for detailed stats. --- ## 3. **RESTCONF / NETCONF (YANG-based APIs)** Modern network devices expose configuration and operational data via RESTCONF (HTTP/JSON) or NETCONF (XML). These APIs are ideal for programmatic access. ### RESTCONF example (Cisco IOS XE) ```http GET https:///restconf/data/Cisco-IOS-XE-native:native/interface/gigabitEthernet=1/description Authorization: Basic Accept: application/yang-data+json ``` ### NETCONF example (Juniper JUNOS) ```xml ``` These calls return structured data that includes all the fields you’d see in a CLI `show interface` command. --- ## 4. **WMI (Windows Management Instrumentation)** For Windows servers or switches running Windows, you can query interface details via PowerShell: ```powershell Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_NetworkAdapterConfiguration | Where-Object {$_.NetEnabled} ``` Output includes IP addresses, MAC, status, etc. --- ## 5. **Using a Network Management System (NMS)** If you’re already using an NMS (e.g., SolarWinds, PRTG, Zabbix, NetBox), most of them automatically poll interfaces via SNMP or agent scripts and present a GUI with all details. You can drill down into a specific interface to see: * Current bandwidth usage * Error rates * Link status history * Configuration snapshots --- ## Quick Checklist for “Detailed Interface Info” 1. **Identify the interface name** (`GigabitEthernet0/1`, `eth0`, `Ethernet0`, etc.). 2. **Choose your method** (CLI, SNMP, RESTCONF, NETCONF, WMI). 3. **Run the command or API call**. 4. **Collect the following key metrics**: * Operational status * Physical status (speed, duplex) * MTU * MAC address * VLANs / sub‑interfaces * Traffic counters (bytes, packets, errors) * Link-layer encapsulation * Any error logs or alarms associated with the interface --- ### Need More Detail? If you tell me: * The vendor and OS (Cisco IOS, Juniper JUNOS, Arista EOS, Linux, Windows, etc.) * Whether you’re on a physical switch/router or a virtual appliance * Your preferred method (CLI vs. API vs. SNMP) I can give you the exact command or API payload, including sample output and how to parse it.
